When new evidence arrives, CUPMem treats it as a potential state update and explicitly adjudicates older memories rather than merely appending the new entry. An LLM-based adjudicator evaluates each candidate old state and decides whether it should remain active, be archived as `STALE`, be replaced, or be marked unresolved (`KEEP`/`STALE`/`REPLACE`/`UNKNOWN`), giving new evidence write-side authority to revise, retire, or block older assumptions before query time [2605.06527#s15.p1]. Memory entries are marked active or stale, and unsafe slots without a settled replacement are marked unknown-current [2605.06527#s15.p1]. If an old item is invalidated its state is written as `STALE`; if only the old default's unsafety is established, the slot is marked `UNKNOWN_CURRENT` [2605.06527#s64.p19]. All such modifications obey a temporal causality constraint: only later evidence may revise or archive earlier items [2605.06527#s64.p19]. Invalidation need not occur in the same slot as the new evidence—CUPMem expands the search to structurally affected state regions via topology-triggered belief propagation [2605.06527#s15.p1]. At query time, active items serve as current grounding, stale items are treated as historical context, and unresolved slots prevent an unsafe old default from being used as a premise [2605.06527#s15.p1].

The two papers report opposite headline results. In the preregistered comparison, the wiki was much better at connecting papers, though its organization advantage fell below the registered threshold [2605.18490#s3.p1][2605.18490#s1.p2]. On the key factor, the preregistered paper attributes disagreement to how the compiled knowledge is served and what is measured: compiled-knowledge architectures "have since been compared against retrieval baselines by several groups, with materially different results depending on how the compiled knowledge is served and what is measured" [2605.18490#s2.p1]. It also stresses that its own systems differ along multiple axes at once (representation, retrieval strategy, test-time compute), so no difference can be attributed to the compiled representation alone [2605.18490#s13.p2][2605.18490#s2.p2]. WiCER's result is framed as a function of corpus scale (80 documents per topic vs the Policygenius setting), with some 80-document corpora even overflowing a 96K context window [2605.07068#s30.p1].

HippoRAG 2 uses its knowledge graph to aid the retrieval process rather than to expand the retrieval corpus itself, which introduces less LLM-generated noise [2502.14802#s5.p3]. Its structural artifact is an explicitly constructed open knowledge graph over which the PPR algorithm is run, integrating passages, queries, and triples [2502.14802#s5.p4].

The LLM Wiki instead compiles the papers offline into a persistent cross-linked markdown wiki (entities, concepts, sources, and analyses with cross-references), and at question time a tool-using agent lists and reads pages to answer [2605.18490#s13.p1]. Its structural artifact is thus a markdown-rendered, cross-linked wiki serving as an intermediate representation [2605.18490#s7.p1].

When new evidence arrives, CUPMem treats it as a potential state update and performs explicit write-side adjudication: an LLM-based adjudicator evaluates each candidate old state and decides whether it should remain active, be archived as `STALE`, be replaced, or be marked unresolved (`KEEP`/`STALE`/`REPLACE`/`UNKNOWN`) [2605.06527#s15.p1]. This gives new evidence write-side authority to revise, retire, or block older assumptions before query time [2605.06527#s15.p1]. If an old item is invalidated, its state is written as `STALE`; if only the old default's unsafety is established, the slot is marked `UNKNOWN_CURRENT` [2605.06527#s64.p19]. Invalidation is not limited to the directly touched slot—it propagates to structurally affected state regions via a bounded candidate set [2605.06527#s15.p1]. All modifications obey a temporal causality constraint: only later evidence may revise or archive earlier memory items [2605.06527#s64.p19]. At query time, active items serve as current grounding, stale items are treated as historical context, and unresolved slots prevent unsafe old defaults from being used as premises [2605.06527#s15.p1].

HippoRAG 2 retrieves over graph-structured long-term memory, incorporating passages into that memory formulation [2607.26604#s3.p2]. The later paper extends WiCER's CEGAR loop by moving from *reactive* counterexample discovery to *proactive* prediction: instead of waiting for a failed QA probe, it predicts likely counterexamples from the news stream and preemptively refines [2606.09877#s11.p1]. The key conceptual shift is that the "counterexample" becomes a high-volatility news item predicted to cause future knowledge gaps, rather than an observed failure [2606.09877#s42.p1]. This is summarized in Table 1 as the shift from "Failed QA probe" to "High-volatility news" (reactive → proactive) and from "Pin missing fact" to "Pin predicted-volatile fact" (diagnosis → prediction) [2606.09877#s42.p3]. The paradigm generalizes to any domain where knowledge gaps can be predicted rather than merely observed, reducing the latency between a gap's emergence and its resolution [2606.09877#s42.p4].

ReFind and Raw-RAG differ in how much agent-controlled, query-time processing they apply over the raw text. ReFind uses the chat archive's existing organization (turn boundaries, session ids, timestamps, raw text) but creates no learned or LLM-generated memory representation; its BM25 index is just an access path, and it defers representation decisions to query time, when the agent knows what evidence it needs [2608.12888#s9.p1]. It maps five failure modes to five mechanisms—reformulation, local expansion, session fusion, temporal filtering, and deduplication—which compose across rounds into an iterative evidence-gathering process [2608.12888#s38.p1]. Raw-RAG likewise avoids LLM-based extraction, summarization, graph construction, or mutation, but its retrieval is a fixed pipeline: serialize with timestamps and captions, split into 256-token windows with 32-token overlap, embed in a flat index, retrieve the 128 closest windows by cosine similarity, then rerank with a cross-encoder to the top 15 for the reader [2610.30755#s6.p2][2610.30755#s6.p3]. So the key difference is that ReFind's retrieval is agent-controlled and iterative (query reformulation and multi-round composition), whereas Raw-RAG's is a single-shot, fixed embed-retrieve-rerank pipeline with no agent-driven query adaptation [2608.12888#s38.p1][2610.30755#s6.p3].

Agent Zero Memory treats a knowledge update as a new, timestamped belief recorded alongside its evidence rather than a destructive overwrite, so the most-recent fact is recoverable with its provenance and the superseded fact remains distinguishable from its correction [2608.29606#s21.p1]. Its Memory Events timeline makes "when" and "what changed" first-class, so a superseded fact is distinguished from its correction rather than returned stale [2608.29606#s10.p1], and nothing is destructive—events accumulate rather than replacing one another, every item carries provenance, and a correction updates belief without erasing what was held [2608.29606#s3.p8]. The design principle emphasized is provenance-aware, layered memory: quality is governed by the structure and provenance of retrieved memory rather than a model's parametric knowledge [2608.29606#s10.p1][2608.29606#s21.p2], and the authors view the provenance-aware, layered memory substrate as the durable abstraction [2608.29606#s22.p1].

Raw-RAG instead challenges the presumed necessity of explicit memory mutation, arguing that capable readers can resolve dynamic states from sufficient raw history and that disabling mutation improves accuracy in the tested configuration [2610.30755#s2.p10]. Its emphasized principle is source-preserving indexing and retrieval with raw evidence as a strong reference baseline—Raw-RAG ranks first in six of seven settings across four benchmarks, matching or exceeding the compared agentic memory systems in most settings [2610.30755#s2.p10], with the pipeline built on source-preserving indexing and retrieval through to evidence assembly [2610.30755#s57.p1].

HippoRAG associates information across passages by building a schemaless knowledge graph as an artificial hippocampal index and running Personalized PageRank seeded on query concepts, which lets it explore KG paths and identify relevant subgraphs for multi-hop reasoning in a single retrieval step [2405.14831#s2.p5]. Its KG and PPR mirror the auto-associative qualities of the hippocampus, with an LLM acting as neocortex and a retrieval encoder linking the two [2502.14802#s7.p1].

TOKI, by contrast, is not a retrieval/association mechanism but a bitemporal operator algebra applied to the LLM-agent write path: it types the operator that decides which of two contradicting facts survives a write and states the isolation level under which that decision is sound [2606.06240#s148.p1]. It builds on the bitemporal data model, multiversion isolation, and K-semiring provenance, fixing the contradiction event the algebra resolves [2606.06240#s5.p1].

In short, HippoRAG's mechanism is graph-based associative retrieval across passages, whereas TOKI's is a typed write-time operator algebra for resolving contradictions under a specified isolation level.

No. The survey frames memory substrates as one of three orthogonal design dimensions without claiming a single dominant substrate [2602.06052#s6.p2], while "Harness the Memory" explicitly states that no single memory design excels along accuracy, efficiency, and cost, motivating a universal adaptive memory system that selects or composes substrates [2608.15008#s2.p1].

HippoRAG integrates new knowledge continuously through its graph-based memory: its "continuously updating nature" and knowledge integration capabilities let it incorporate new information into the KG index rather than relying on parametric memory [2405.14831#s21.p1]. GC-Mem, by contrast, handles conflicting information by *excising* contradictory old chunks from memory rather than re-ranking them, which is why it retains a substantial advantage over timestamp re-ranking [2609.16073#s14.p4]. GC-Mem's efficacy depends on a detector with high recall (>50%) to identify conflicts [2609.16073#s16.p2], and its success is bounded by the underlying model's reasoning capabilities [2609.16073#s16.p1].

The paper is **RAPTOR: Recursive Abstractive Processing for Tree-Organized Retrieval**. It clusters chunks of text, generates summaries of those clusters, and repeats this bottom-up to build a tree, enabling the LLM to load chunks representing the text at different levels so it can answer questions at different levels [2401.18059#s2.p4]. The recursive cycle of embedding, clustering, and summarization continues until further clustering becomes infeasible, producing a multi-layered tree [2401.18059#s8.p3].

The GraphRAG paper: it builds an entity knowledge graph, partitions it into a hierarchy of communities of closely related entities, and pregenerates community summaries, then answers global queries via map-reduce over those summaries [2404.16130#s1.p1] [2404.16130#s2.p3].
